findings.mechanism: size_orders converts notional into shares by dividing by panel["close"], and net_return credits the position the full close_to_close move. Together these say every order is filled exactly at the closing print. The only offsetting charge is turnover * COST_BPS / 1e4 with COST_BPS = 2.0, a commission-scale number that does not cover half a bid-ask spread outside the most liquid large caps. Because it is a fixed bp rate on |dw| it is invariant to the `capital` argument, so doubling the book size charges no extra impact.
findings.title: Orders filled at the closing print with only a flat 2bp charge

findings.mechanism: size_orders computes notional = weight * capital and returns notional / close as a share count. `capital` is an unconstrained caller-supplied float and the share count grows linearly with it without bound. No volume, ADV or participation-rate column is read anywhere in this module, and no cap is applied, so whatever share count comes out is assumed filled in full at that day's close. This panel spans the small- and mid-cap names where such an order can be a multiple of a day's traded volume, and those are exactly the names an earnings-yield signal tends to select. Capacity is unbounded by construction.
findings.title: Order sizing scales with capital and never checks against traded volume

findings.mechanism: add_label defines the target as intraday_move = close_t / open_t - 1. add_features then builds close_to_close = close_t / close_{t-1} - 1 on the same bar t. Both use close_t, the very price whose realisation the label measures. The leak is exact rather than partial: line 52 supplies overnight_gap = open_t / close_{t-1} - 1, so (1 + close_to_close) / (1 + overnight_gap) - 1 = the label. Two columns reconstruct the target arithmetically with no residual. There is no gap between the feature bar and the label horizon - they are the same bar.
findings.title: Same-bar close return makes the intraday label algebraically recoverable

findings.mechanism: realised_vol is a 60-bar rolling std of close.pct_change(). pandas' rolling window is inclusive of the current row, so the value at bar t is computed over returns up to and including close_t. close_t is the terminal price of the label, so the magnitude of the very move being predicted is one of the 60 observations feeding the dispersion estimate. A window ending at bar t-1 would be the observable version.
findings.title: Trailing volatility window includes the label bar's own return

findings.mechanism: load_fundamentals parses both `period_end` and `filing_date`, and its own docstring states that `filing_date` is the day the report was actually released, "typically six to nine weeks later" than the quarter end. attach_fundamentals then joins the daily panel's `date` against `period_end`, so every quarterly figure lands on the panel row for the last day of the quarter and, after the ffill on line 37, is carried forward from that day onward. A person standing on the quarter-end bar had not seen the report yet. The available `filing_date` column - the only date that represents availability rather than effectivity - is never used as a join key or a mask.
findings.title: Fundamentals joined on period_end rather than filing_date

findings.mechanism: add_label defines the target as `intraday_move = close/open - 1` for the same session, so the decision point for row t is that session's open. `close_to_close` at row t embeds `close[t]` - the numerator of the label for that same row. Combined with `overnight_gap`, this feature reconstructs the target algebraically: intraday_move = (1+close_to_close)/(1+overnight_gap) - 1. Nothing here is a mechanical forward shift; the leak comes from the label being intraday while the feature is measured at the closing print.
findings.title: close_to_close feature contains the same session's close, which is the label

findings.mechanism: The window is trailing, which is why a pattern-matcher passes it, but its right edge sits on bar t. The 60-observation rolling std at row t includes `close[t]`. Because the label is the same session's open-to-close move, the decision time for row t is the open of t, at which point `close[t]` has not printed. The feature is contaminated specifically by the magnitude of the move the model is asked to predict.
findings.title: Trailing volatility window includes the return of the bar it labels

findings.mechanism: The frame is sorted by ticker then date and forward-filled with no `groupby("ticker")`. At each ticker boundary the last row of ticker A is its most recent date, while the first rows of ticker B are the beginning of the sample. pandas' ffill does not know about the boundary, so ticker A's end-of-sample fundamentals are propagated into ticker B's earliest bars. Those values are both from a different issuer and from a calendar date years after the bar receiving them.
findings.title: Frame-wide ffill leaks one ticker's later fundamentals into another ticker's earlier rows

findings.mechanism: The docstring states `reference` is one row per ticker, so it has no effective date. Joining on `ticker` alone stamps the current classification onto every historical bar. A company reclassified, redomiciled, or uplisted is labelled with its post-change attributes across its entire pre-change history. At bar t only the then-current classification was knowable.
findings.title: Sector reference joined on ticker alone carries today's classification back over all history

findings.mechanism: `attach_sector` joins `reference` - documented as one row per ticker: sector, country, listing venue - onto the time-indexed daily panel on `ticker` alone, with no date dimension. Every row of a ticker's history receives the single stored value. Those are exactly the attributes that change over a company's life: sector reclassifications, redomiciliation, and venue moves. A one-row-per-ticker table can only hold the value as of whenever it was extracted, which is after the end of the sample. It becomes an outright survivorship filter if any downstream step drops rows with missing sector, since names delisted before the snapshot are the ones most likely to be absent.
findings.title: Point-in-time-less sector reference joined onto the whole daily panel

findings.mechanism: `split` builds folds with GroupKFold using groups=panel["ticker"], so the only axis the splitter respects is the name. Nothing references `date` or orders rows in time. Every fold spans the full calendar history: while ticker A is held out, tickers B..Z are in the training fold over exactly the same sessions. The label is dominated by that session's common market and sector move, so the model can learn the realised factor return of a date from the training tickers and apply it to the held-out ticker on that same date. No calendar day is ever purged and there is no embargo, because the splitter has no notion of a time boundary.
findings.title: GroupKFold grouped by ticker ignores the date axis entirely

findings.mechanism: ROUNDS records the configuration changes that produced the headline number, and report's docstring states the writeup uses round 5. Round 5's change is dropping the two sectors that turned out worst. 'Worst-performing' is a ranking over realised returns across the study period, including the holdout that begins at HOLDOUT_START and is the very window report scores on. Nothing computes that ranking from data ending before the holdout, so the names remaining are exactly those whose sectors are already known to have done well. The Sharpe jump from 0.71 to 0.94 is the size of that selection effect, not an improvement in the model.
findings.title: Round 5 universe excludes the two worst-performing sectors, a whole-sample outcome

findings.mechanism: ROUNDS records five successive model revisions, each scored on the period returned by holdout(), which is always the same fixed slice. The Sharpe column climbs monotonically 0.31 to 0.94 precisely because each change was kept or discarded on the basis of the previous round's holdout number: round 3 dropped what round 2 added, round 4 widened a window, and round 5 excluded the two worst-performing sectors - worst-performing on the holdout itself, a parameter fitted directly to the evaluation data. report() then returns that fifth configuration's holdout Sharpe as the headline. There is no sweep object and no explicit grid, so nothing mechanical fires, but the researcher has performed a five-trial search with the holdout as the objective, and no untouched period remains.
findings.quoted_line: """Headline number for the writeup: round 5, evaluated on the holdout."""
findings.title: Headline Sharpe is the fifth revision scored on the same holdout used to choose all five
